shortQuestions: Aliphatic hydrocarbons are open-chain (or non-aromatic cyclic) hydrocarbons — alkanes, alkenes, alkynes and cycloalkanes; unsaturated ones readily undergo addition reactions.

Aromatic hydrocarbons contain one or more benzene rings with a delocalised ring of π electrons (4n + 2 π electrons); they are unusually stable and prefer substitution to addition, e.g. benzene, toluene, naphthalene.
Plane-polarised light is light whose electric vibrations occur in only one plane. Monochromatic light has a single wavelength (e.g. the sodium D line, 589 nm).

Plane-polarised monochromatic light is produced by passing light from a sodium lamp through a Nicol prism or Polaroid; it is used in a polarimeter to measure the optical rotation of chiral (optically active) compounds.
Bromine water (or Br₂ in CCl₄) test: the reddish-brown colour is discharged rapidly as bromine adds across the C=C bond: CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → CH₂Br–CH₂Br.
Baeyer's test: cold, dilute alkaline KMnO₄ loses its purple colour and a brown precipitate of MnO₂ forms as the alkene is oxidised to a diol.

In benzene the six π electrons are delocalised over the ring, giving a resonance (aromatic) stabilisation of about 150 kJ mol⁻¹; addition would destroy this, so benzene is less reactive than ethene, whose localised π electrons are easily attacked.
However benzene still has a cloud of π electrons available for electrophiles (it undergoes substitution), whereas ethane has only strong σ bonds; so benzene is more reactive than ethane.
Halogens are highly electronegative: they withdraw electron density from the ring by the inductive (−I) effect, making it less reactive than benzene — so they are deactivating.

But their lone pairs are donated into the ring by resonance (+R), increasing electron density at the ortho and para positions and stabilising the arenium ions formed by o/p attack — so they are ortho/para directing.
A chiral carbon (asymmetric carbon, stereocentre) is a carbon atom attached to four different atoms or groups.

Chirality is a property of the whole molecule: it is non-superimposable on its mirror image. Usually a chiral carbon makes a molecule chiral, but a molecule may be chiral without one (some allenes and biphenyls) or achiral despite having them (meso compounds).
But-1-ene is CH₂=CH–CH₂CH₃. Carbon-1 of the double bond carries two identical hydrogen atoms.
Geometrical (cis–trans) isomerism needs two different groups on each double-bonded carbon, so but-1-ene has no geometrical isomers.
In cyclopropane the C–C–C angle is 60°, far from the normal tetrahedral angle of 109.5°; this causes large angle strain (Baeyer strain) and poor overlap of orbitals (bent 'banana' bonds).
These weak, strained bonds break easily; ring opening relieves the strain, so cyclopropane undergoes addition reactions (with H₂, Br₂, HBr) that propane does not.
Terminal (1-)alkynes have an acidic hydrogen on the triple-bonded carbon (≡C–H).
With ammoniacal silver nitrate they give a white precipitate of a silver alkynide, and with ammoniacal copper(I) chloride a red precipitate: HC≡CH + 2[Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ → AgC≡CAg↓ + 2NH₄⁺ + 2NH₃.
Non-terminal alkynes (e.g. but-2-yne) give no precipitate.
Tautomerism: two real, separable isomers exist in dynamic equilibrium and differ in the position of an atom (usually H) as well as of electrons, e.g. keto ⇌ enol forms of acetoacetic ester.

Resonance: a single real molecule is represented by several structures that differ only in the arrangement of electrons, not of atoms; the contributing structures do not exist separately — the real molecule is their hybrid (e.g. benzene).
longQuestions: (a) Chlorination of methane is a free-radical chain reaction in UV light or at 300 °C. Initiation: Cl₂ → 2Cl•. Propagation: Cl• + CH₄ → •CH₃ + HCl; •CH₃ + Cl₂ → CH₃Cl + Cl• (the Cl• continues the chain). Termination: Cl• + Cl• → Cl₂; •CH₃ + Cl• → CH₃Cl; •CH₃ + •CH₃ → C₂H₆. With excess chlorine, further substitution gives CH₂Cl₂, CHCl₃ and CCl₄.

(b) Cycloalkanes (CₙH₂ₙ) are saturated ring hydrocarbons. In cyclopropane (60°) and cyclobutane (≈ 90°) the bond angles are much smaller than 109.5°, causing angle strain; they are reactive and undergo ring-opening addition (e.g. cyclopropane + H₂/Ni → propane; + Br₂ → 1,3-dibromopropane). Cyclopentane and cyclohexane (puckered 'chair' form, 109.5° angles) are almost strain-free and react like alkanes, by substitution.

(c) Physical properties of alkanes and cycloalkanes: non-polar, colourless; insoluble in water but soluble in organic solvents; less dense than water. C₁–C₄ are gases, C₅–C₁₇ liquids and higher members waxy solids. Boiling points rise with molecular mass (stronger van der Waals forces) and fall with branching. Cycloalkanes have higher boiling points, melting points and densities than the corresponding open-chain alkanes.

(a) Hydrocarbons are compounds containing only carbon and hydrogen. Classes: (i) aliphatic (open-chain) — saturated alkanes CₙH₂ₙ₊₂ (methane, ethane) and unsaturated alkenes CₙH₂ₙ (ethene) and alkynes CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ (ethyne); (ii) alicyclic — cycloalkanes and cycloalkenes (cyclohexane); (iii) aromatic — benzene and its homologues (benzene, toluene, naphthalene).
(b)(i) Dehydration of ethyl alcohol with excess concentrated H₂SO₄ at 170 °C (or Al₂O₃ at 350 °C): CH₃CH₂OH → CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O.
(ii) Dehydrohalogenation of ethyl bromide by boiling with alcoholic KOH: CH₃CH₂Br + KOH(alc) → CH₂=CH₂ + KBr + H₂O.

(c) Relative stability of alkenes (from heats of hydrogenation): the more alkyl groups attached to the double-bonded carbons, the more stable the alkene (hyperconjugation and inductive donation): R₂C=CR₂ > R₂C=CHR > R₂C=CH₂ ≈ RCH=CHR > RCH=CH₂ > CH₂=CH₂. Trans-alkenes are more stable than cis-alkenes because the bulky groups are farther apart (less steric strain).

(a) Preparation of alkynes: (i) Dehydrohalogenation of vicinal dihalides with alcoholic KOH (then NaNH₂): CH₂Br–CH₂Br + 2KOH → HC≡CH + 2KBr + 2H₂O. (ii) Dehalogenation of tetrahalides with zinc: CHBr₂–CHBr₂ + 2Zn → HC≡CH + 2ZnBr₂. (Also: CaC₂ + 2H₂O → HC≡CH + Ca(OH)₂.)

(b) Acidity: the ≡C–H carbon is sp-hybridised (50% s-character), so it is more electronegative and holds the bonding pair closer, letting H leave as H⁺ (pKa ≈ 25, more acidic than alkenes and alkanes). Terminal alkynes form salts: HC≡CH + NaNH₂ → HC≡C⁻Na⁺ + NH₃; 2HC≡CH + 2Na → 2HC≡CNa + H₂. Distinction: terminal alkynes give a white precipitate with ammoniacal AgNO₃ and a red precipitate with ammoniacal Cu₂Cl₂; non-terminal alkynes do not.

(c) From an alkene (ethene as example): (i) vicinal dihalide — add Br₂ in CCl₄: CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → CH₂Br–CH₂Br. (ii) Alcohol — hydration with dilute H₂SO₄ (or via concentrated H₂SO₄ then water): CH₂=CH₂ + H₂O → CH₃CH₂OH. (iii) Aldehydes and ketones — ozonolysis: alkene + O₃ → ozonide, then Zn/H₂O, e.g. CH₃CH=CHCH₃ → 2CH₃CHO; (CH₃)₂C=C(CH₃)₂ → 2(CH₃)₂CO. (iv) Epoxide — catalytic oxidation of ethene with O₂ over Ag at about 250 °C, or reaction with a peroxyacid: CH₂=CH₂ + ½O₂ → ethylene oxide (oxirane).

(a) Molecular-orbital structure: each carbon is sp²-hybridised; sp² orbitals form C–C σ bonds and C–H σ bonds at 120°, making a flat hexagonal ring. Each carbon also has an unhybridised 2p orbital perpendicular to the ring. The six p orbitals overlap sideways all round the ring to form six π molecular orbitals; the three bonding MOs hold the six π electrons, which are delocalised as two rings of electron density above and below the plane. Hence all C–C bonds are equal (139 pm) and benzene has extra (resonance) stability of about 150 kJ mol⁻¹.

(b) Electrophilic substitution mechanism: (1) Generation of the electrophile, e.g. HNO₃ + 2H₂SO₄ → NO₂⁺ + H₃O⁺ + 2HSO₄⁻. (2) The electrophile attacks the π cloud, forming a resonance-stabilised arenium ion (σ-complex) — the slow, rate-determining step. (3) A base (HSO₄⁻) removes H⁺ from the sp³ carbon, restoring the aromatic ring: C₆H₆ + NO₂⁺ → C₆H₅NO₂ + H⁺.

(c) (i) Acetophenone (Friedel–Crafts acylation): C₆H₆ + CH₃COCl —AlCl₃→ C₆H₅COCH₃ + HCl. (ii) Toluene (Friedel–Crafts alkylation): C₆H₆ + CH₃Cl —AlCl₃→ C₆H₅CH₃ + HCl. (iii) Nitrobenzene: C₆H₆ + HNO₃ —conc. H₂SO₄, 50–55 °C→ C₆H₅NO₂ + H₂O. (iv) Benzenesulphonic acid: C₆H₆ + H₂SO₄ (fuming, SO₃) → C₆H₅SO₃H + H₂O. (v) Chlorobenzene: C₆H₆ + Cl₂ —FeCl₃→ C₆H₅Cl + HCl. (vi) Cyclohexane: C₆H₆ + 3H₂ —Ni, 150–200 °C→ C₆H₁₂.

(a) A substituent already on a benzene ring decides how fast and where a second group enters. Activating ortho/para directors donate electrons (+R or +I): –OH, –NH₂, –OR, –NHCOCH₃, –CH₃; they make the ring more reactive than benzene and stabilise the arenium ions for ortho/para attack. Deactivating meta directors withdraw electrons (−R, −I): –NO₂, –CN, –CHO, –COOH, –SO₃H, –CF₃; they make the ring less reactive, and ortho/para attack is especially destabilised, so substitution occurs at meta. Halogens are deactivating (−I) but ortho/para directing (+R). E.g. phenol nitrates easily at o/p; nitrobenzene nitrates slowly at meta.

(b) Structural (condensed) formulas: (i) 3-ethyl-4-methyloctane: CH₃CH₂CH(C₂H₅)CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₂CH₂CH₃. (ii) 4-isopropyldecane: CH₃CH₂CH₂CH[CH(CH₃)₂](CH₂)₅CH₃. (iii) sec-butylcycloheptane: a cycloheptane ring carrying –CH(CH₃)CH₂CH₃. (iv) 2,3-dimethyl-4-propylnonane: CH₃CH(CH₃)CH(CH₃)CH(CH₂CH₂CH₃)(CH₂)₄CH₃.

(iv) 2,4,4-trimethylhex-2-ene: (CH₃)₂C=CH–C(CH₃)₂–CH₂CH₃. (v) cis-hex-3-ene: CH₃CH₂–CH=CH–CH₂CH₃ with both ethyl groups on the same side of the double bond. (vi) Phenanthrene: C₁₄H₁₀, three benzene rings fused in an angular arrangement. (vii) Hex-2-yne: CH₃C≡CCH₂CH₂CH₃.
(viii) 1,2-dimethyl-4-propylbenzene: a benzene ring with CH₃ groups at C1 and C2 and –CH₂CH₂CH₃ at C4. (ix) Cyclopropylbenzene: C₆H₅–C₃H₅ (a phenyl group attached to a cyclopropane ring).
activities: Observation: the brown (or yellow-brown) colour of the bromine reagent disappears almost at once, drop after drop, until the C=C bonds are used up.
Reason: bromine adds across the carbon–carbon double bond to form a colourless vicinal dibromide, e.g. CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → CH₂Br–CH₂Br.
Conclusion: rapid decolourisation shows unsaturation (C=C or C≡C). A saturated compound leaves the brown colour unchanged (without UV light).
